segments.t: Disaster strikes when the thrown coconut hits the Michelin inspector instead of Senya. When the terrified inspector wakes up, Chef Barinov desperately tries to calm him down and asks Fedya to escort him to his room.
Хотите пойти к себе в номер?
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
'Chef, those were just coconuts.' Fedya continues wryly during the talk, steering the talk right where he wants it.
'Be quiet right now, Fedya!' Barinov counters naturally on the spot and puts the weight on "zamolchi" ("to fall silent", from "zamolchat") as the exchange unfolds.
'I will bring him to his senses now.' Talking about the feeling right here, Fedya brings in "chuvstvo" ("feeling, emotion") to make the meaning unmistakable.
'Stand right there!' Barinov responds candidly watching Fedya, shifting the mood of the conversation in a single beat.
'Chef, excuse me, please.' Fedya warmly chooses this polite apology at this moment using "izvinite" ("excuse me") — the respectful form of "excuse me" or "sorry" used when stepping in or apologizing.

'Please do not kill me.' The inspector calmly sends this courtesy word at this moment using "pozhaluysta" ("please") — the all-purpose Russian politeness word that covers both "please" and "you're welcome".
'We do not wish you any harm.' Barinov opens up promptly toward the inspector, refusing to let the moment slip past.
'Then why did you hit me?' The inspector replies boldly in this beat and puts the weight on "udarili" ("to hit, to strike", from "udarit") as the exchange unfolds.
'This is just a foolish misunderstanding.' Pointing to a foolish misunderstanding in the exchange, Barinov uses the little word "prosto" ("simply, just") to make the point sound effortless.

'Let me go from here, please.' The inspector plainly uses this courtesy word to Barinov using "pozhaluysta" ("please") — the all-purpose Russian politeness word that covers both "please" and "you're welcome".

'Of course, you are completely free.' Barinov calmly shares this confirmation while facing the inspector using "konechno" ("of course") — spoken with a soft "shn" sound in everyday Moscow Russian to mean "of course, certainly".
Хотите пойти к себе в номер?
'Do you want to go to your room?' Pointing to the number in this beat, Barinov keeps normal statement word order here, turning the line into a question for the inspector purely through rising pitch.

'Fedya, escort the man, please.' Barinov promptly offers this courtesy word in front of Fedya using "pozhaluysta" ("please") — the all-purpose Russian politeness word that covers both "please" and "you're welcome".
Хотите пойти к себе в номер?
Chef Barinov only meant for Fedya to walk the shaken inspector to his hotel room, but Fedya misinterprets the order in the worst possible way. Until next time!
